title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: When someone lends out stock at interest, they always treat it as capital. They expect it back in due course, and in the meantime they expect the borrower to pay them a fixed annual rent for the use of it. The borrower can put it to one of two uses: as capital, or as a fund set aside for immediate consumption. If the borrower uses it as capital, they spend it maintaining productive workers, who reproduce its value and add a profit. In that case the borrower can both repay the capital and pay the interest without drawing on or eating into any other source of income. But if the borrower treats it as a fund for immediate consumption, they behave like a spendthrift: they squander on idle people what was meant to support productive ones. In that case the borrower can neither repay the capital nor pay the interest without drawing on or eating into some other source of income, such as land or the rent it brings in.

Lent stock is, of course, sometimes used in both ways, but far more often in the first than the second. Anyone who borrows in order to spend will soon be ruined, and the lender will usually have reason to regret the foolishness of having lent to them. So borrowing or lending for that purpose, in every case where outright extortion is not the point, runs against the interest of both parties. It does happen now and then that people do both, but because everyone cares about their own interest, we can be confident it does not happen nearly as often as we sometimes imagine. Ask any reasonably prudent rich man which of the two kinds of people he has lent most of his stock to: those he expects to use it profitably, or those he expects to fritter it away. He will laugh at you for even asking. So even among borrowers, who are not exactly famous for thrift, the frugal and hardworking far outnumber the spendthrift and idle.

The only people who are routinely lent stock without any expectation that they will use it profitably are country gentlemen who borrow against a mortgage. And even they hardly ever borrow simply to spend. What they borrow has, you might say, usually been spent before they borrow it. They have generally run up such large bills for goods supplied on credit by shopkeepers and tradesmen that they need to take out an interest-bearing loan just to settle the debt. The borrowed capital replaces the capital of those shopkeepers and tradesmen, which the country gentlemen could not have replaced out of the rents of their estates. So it is not really borrowed in order to be spent, but in order to replace a capital that had already been spent.

Almost all interest-bearing loans are made in money, whether paper or gold and silver. But what the borrower actually wants, and what the lender is happy to supply, is not the money itself but its purchasing power, the goods it can buy. If the borrower wants it as a fund for immediate consumption, only those goods can go into that fund. If the borrower wants it as capital to employ workers, only those goods can supply the workers with the tools, materials, and provisions they need to do their work. Through the loan, the lender in effect signs over to the borrower a claim to a certain share of the country's annual produce of land and labour, for the borrower to use as they see fit.

So the amount of stock, or as people usually put it, of money, that can be lent at interest in any country is not set by the value of the money, paper or coin, that serves as the vehicle for the various loans made there. It is set by the value of that part of the annual produce which, as soon as it comes either from the ground or from the hands of productive workers, is destined not just to replace a capital, but to replace a capital that its owner would rather not bother employing personally. Since such capitals are usually lent and repaid in money, they make up what is called the monied interest. This is distinct not only from the landed interest but from the trading and manufacturing interests, because in those last two the owners employ their own capital themselves. Even within the monied interest, though, the money is only the deed of transfer, conveying from one person to another the capitals their owners would rather not employ. Those capitals can be many times larger than the amount of money that serves to convey them, because the same coins can be used in turn for many different loans, just as they can for many different purchases. Suppose A lends W £1000, and W immediately uses it to buy £1000 worth of goods from B. B has no need of the money, so he lends the very same coins to X, who immediately buys £1000 worth of goods from C. C does the same, for the same reason, lending them to Y, who again buys goods with them from D. In this way the same coins or notes can, within a few days, serve as the vehicle for three different loans and three different purchases, each one worth the full amount of those coins. What the three monied men, A, B, and C, transferred to the three borrowers, W, X, and Y, is the power to make those purchases. That power is exactly where the value and the use of the loans lie. The stock lent by the three monied men equals the value of the goods that can be bought with it, which is three times the value of the money used to buy them. Yet those loans can all be perfectly secure, because the goods bought by the various debtors are put to work so as to bring back, in due time and at a profit, an equal value in coin or notes. And just as the same coins can serve as the vehicle for loans worth three times, or by the same logic thirty times, their own value, so too they can serve in turn as the vehicle for repaying them.

A capital lent at interest can therefore be seen as a transfer, from lender to borrower, of a sizeable share of the annual produce, on condition that the borrower in return hands over to the lender each year, for as long as the loan runs, a small share called the interest, and at the end hands over a share as large as the one originally transferred, called the repayment. Money, whether coin or paper, generally serves as the deed of transfer for both the smaller and the larger share, but the money itself is something entirely different from what it transfers.

As the share of the annual produce that is destined, the moment it comes from the ground or from productive workers, to replace a capital grows larger in any country, the so-called monied interest naturally grows with it. The increase in those particular capitals whose owners want an income from them without the trouble of employing them naturally goes hand in hand with the general increase of capital. In other words, as stock increases, the amount of stock available to be lent at interest grows steadily larger.

As the amount of stock available to lend at interest grows, the interest, the price that must be paid for using that stock, necessarily falls. This happens partly for the general reason that the market price of anything usually drops as its quantity rises, and partly for reasons peculiar to this case. As capital increases in a country, the profit that can be made by employing it necessarily falls. It becomes harder and harder to find a profitable way of employing any new capital within the country. The result is competition between different capitals, with the owner of one trying to take over the line of business occupied by another. In most cases he can only hope to elbow that other out by offering better terms. He must not only sell his goods somewhat cheaper, but, in order to get them to sell, he must sometimes buy them dearer too. Meanwhile, as the funds set aside to maintain productive labour grow, the demand for that labour grows greater every day. Workers easily find jobs, while the owners of capital struggle to find workers to employ. Their competition pushes up wages and pushes down the profits of stock. And when the profit that can be made from a capital is squeezed in this way at both ends, the price that can be paid for using it, that is, the rate of interest, must necessarily fall along with it.

Mr Locke, Mr Law, and Mr Montesquieu, along with many other writers, seem to have thought that the increase in the quantity of gold and silver after the discovery of the Spanish West Indies was the real reason interest rates fell across most of Europe. Their argument runs that since the metals themselves became less valuable, the use of any given portion of them necessarily became less valuable too, and so did the price that could be paid for it. This idea looks plausible at first, but Mr Hume has exposed its flaws so thoroughly that there is perhaps little need to say more. Still, the following very short and simple argument may help to spell out more clearly the mistake that seems to have misled these gentlemen.

Before the discovery of the Spanish West Indies, ten per cent seems to have been the usual rate of interest across most of Europe. Since then it has fallen, in various countries, to six, five, four, and three per cent. Suppose that in each country the value of silver fell in exactly the same proportion as the rate of interest, so that in countries where interest dropped from ten to five per cent, the same quantity of silver now buys just half the goods it could buy before. I do not believe this assumption holds true anywhere, but it is the one most favourable to the view we are about to test. Even on this assumption, it is completely impossible that the fall in the value of silver could have had the slightest tendency to lower the rate of interest. If £100 in those countries is now worth no more than £50 was then, then £10 must now be worth no more than £5 was then. Whatever caused the value of the capital to fall must have lowered the value of the interest as well, and in exactly the same proportion. The ratio between the value of the capital and the value of the interest would have stayed the same, even if the rate had never changed at all. Changing the rate, by contrast, necessarily changes that ratio. If £100 now is worth no more than £50 was then, then £5 now can be worth no more than £2 10s. was then. So by cutting the interest rate from ten to five per cent, we are paying, for the use of a capital supposedly worth half its former value, an interest worth only a quarter of the former interest.

An increase in the quantity of silver, while the quantity of goods it circulated stayed the same, could do nothing except lower the value of the metal. The nominal price of all goods would be higher, but their real value would be exactly the same as before. They would exchange for more pieces of silver, but the amount of labour they could command, and the number of people they could support and employ, would be exactly the same. The country's capital would be the same, even if more coins were needed to move any given portion of it from one hand to another. The deeds of transfer, like the documents of a long-winded lawyer, would be more cumbersome, but the thing transferred would be exactly the same as before, and could produce only the same results. Since the funds for maintaining productive labour would be the same, the demand for it would be the same too. So its price, or wages, though nominally higher, would really be the same. They would be paid in more pieces of silver, but those pieces would buy only the same quantity of goods. The profits of stock would be the same, both nominally and really. Wages are usually reckoned by the quantity of silver paid to the worker, so when that goes up his wages look as though they have risen, even though they may be no greater than before. But the profits of stock are not reckoned by the number of silver pieces in which they are paid, but by the proportion those pieces bear to the whole capital employed. So in a given country, 5s. a week might be the usual wage of labour and ten per cent the usual profit of stock; but with the country's whole capital unchanged, the competition between the various individual capitals it is divided into would also be unchanged. They would all trade with the same advantages and disadvantages. So the usual ratio between capital and profit would stay the same, and consequently so would the usual interest on money, since what can normally be paid for the use of money is necessarily governed by what can normally be made by using it.

Any increase in the quantity of goods circulated within the country each year, while the quantity of money circulating them stayed the same, would by contrast produce many other important effects besides raising the value of the money. The country's capital, though nominally the same, would really be larger. It might still be expressed by the same quantity of money, but it would command a greater quantity of labour. The amount of productive labour it could support and employ would increase, and so would the demand for that labour. Wages would naturally rise with the demand, and yet might appear to fall. They might be paid in a smaller quantity of money, but that smaller quantity might buy a greater quantity of goods than a larger one had before. The profits of stock would fall, both really and in appearance. With the country's whole capital larger, the competition between the various capitals making it up would naturally grow along with it. The owners of those particular capitals would have to settle for a smaller share of the produce of the labour their capitals employed. The interest on money, always keeping pace with the profits of stock, could in this way be greatly reduced, even while the value of money, the quantity of goods any given sum could buy, was greatly increased.

In some countries the law has banned interest on money altogether. But since money can be made to earn something everywhere, something ought everywhere to be paid for its use. This rule, far from preventing the evil of usury, has been found by experience to make it worse. The debtor has to pay not only for the use of the money but also for the risk the creditor takes by accepting any payment for that use. In effect, the debtor has to insure the creditor against the penalties for usury.

In countries where interest is allowed, the law usually fixes the highest rate that can be charged without penalty, in order to prevent extortionate usury. That rate should always be set somewhat above the lowest market price, the price usually paid for the use of money by borrowers who can offer the most unquestionable security. If the legal rate were set below the lowest market rate, the effects would be almost the same as banning interest outright. The creditor will not lend his money for less than its use is worth, so the debtor must pay him for the risk he runs in accepting the full value of that use. If the legal rate were set exactly at the lowest market price, it would ruin, among honest people who respect their country's laws, the credit of everyone who cannot offer the very best security, forcing them to turn to extortionate lenders. In a country like Great Britain, where money is lent to the government at three per cent and to private individuals on good security at four or four and a half, the present legal rate of five per cent is perhaps as suitable as any.

It should be noted that the legal rate, though it ought to be somewhat above the lowest market rate, ought not to be much above it. If the legal rate of interest in Great Britain, say, were set as high as eight or ten per cent, most of the money available for lending would go to spendthrifts and speculators, who would be the only ones willing to pay such high interest. Sober people, who will pay for the use of money no more than a fraction of what they expect to make by using it, would not enter the competition. So a large part of the country's capital would be kept out of the hands most likely to use it profitably and advantageously, and thrown into the hands most likely to waste and destroy it. Where the legal rate is set only very slightly above the lowest market rate, on the other hand, sober people are everywhere preferred as borrowers over spendthrifts and speculators. The lender gets nearly as much interest from the former as he dares to charge the latter, and his money is much safer with the first sort of people than with the second. So a large part of the country's capital is thrown into the hands most likely to employ it advantageously.

No law can push the usual rate of interest below the lowest ordinary market rate at the time the law is made. Despite the edict of 1766, by which the French king tried to cut the rate of interest from five to four per cent, money continued to be lent in France at five per cent, the law being dodged in various ways.

It should be noted that the ordinary market price of land depends everywhere on the ordinary market rate of interest. A person with capital who wants an income from it without the trouble of employing it himself weighs whether to buy land with it or lend it out at interest. The greater security of land, along with some other advantages that almost always come with this kind of property, will generally lead him to settle for a smaller income from land than he could get by lending his money at interest. These advantages are enough to make up for a certain gap in income, but only a certain gap. If the rent of land fell short of the interest on money by more than that, nobody would buy land, which would soon bring its ordinary price down. On the other hand, if the advantages more than made up for the gap, everybody would buy land, which would soon push its ordinary price up. When interest was at ten per cent, land usually sold for ten or twelve years' purchase. As interest sank to six, five, and four per cent, the price of land rose to twenty, twenty-five, and thirty years' purchase. The market rate of interest is higher in France than in England, and the usual price of land is lower. In England it usually sells at thirty years' purchase, in France at twenty.
